Business Partner's Corner

​

3 Magic Business Partnership Questions

​

Sticking with the theme of asking great questions, here are three impactful questions that can help you become a fantastic business partner.

​

1. How can I help?

​

​

Jamie Chiarotto is now the CEO of Skjodt-Barrett foods in Toronto. When I worked with him at Kraft Foods, I witnessed his amazing ability to connect with all stakeholders. Folks who were more senior than him. Folks who were in different functions. Folks who were more junior than him. He shot up the corporate ladder and is still thriving today.

​

I asked him what the secret of success was. He shared these 4 magic words (how can I help?). He would always ask that question and then DELIVER!

​

Even stakeholders who initially resisted his attempts to build a bridge eventually warmed up when they knew he saw wanted to help. A simple question that can lead to partnership breakthroughs. This was a wonderful way for him to WEDGE himself into the partnering relationship.

​

​

​
​2. WIIFT – what’s in it for them?

​

Many years ago, I was doing a 20-page cost review presentation for my general manager and was putting him to sleep. I remember starting to review the deck with him and seeing him physically back away and disengage. I plowed forward and reviewed the deck with him with very little engagement from him.

​

He gave my manager feedback that I was not cutting it. I was not providing value added support. I was extremely frustrated as I was putting in a tremendous amount of work. The challenge was that I was not considering his perspective. I was approaching it purely from my own point of view.

​

One of my mentors provided some great advice which was WIIFT (what is in it for them?). He simply wanted a one pager that helped him understand if we were on or off track (a simple thumbs up or thumbs down). If we were off track, what could we do about it.

​

I stopped doing the 20-page deck and switched to a one pager and VOILA. I moved from ‘not cutting it’ to ‘exceeding expectations’ when I started approaching it from his perspective.

​

​

​3. How can I simplify?

In my 20 years in Finance, I remember several meetings where jargon was being tossed around like it was going out of style.

​

Inventory revaluation, EBITDA, write-off, depreciation, amortization…. the list goes on.

​

Often times, our cross-functional partners have no idea what we are talking about. A simple solution becomes to avoid jargon wherever possible. If you have to use jargon or acronyms, take time to explain them in business terms. Your stakeholders will appreciate it and you will move closer to being a great business partner.

​

Whenever possible, SIMPLIFY, SIMPLIFY, SIMPLIFY!

​

These three questions are magical when it comes to business partnership!

The FP&A Guy's Tech Tips

​

The rapid advancement of AI is amazing. I am contacted nearly weekly by someone starting an AI-focused software company. It shows how quickly AI has become a daily part of our lives. ​

​

Just this week Apple announced Apple Intelligence and how it will infuse AI much more deeply in its cellphones. ​ ​ While it might be true that the use cases in Finance are not as broad as other parts of the business they are growing, and they are there even today. ​ These use cases will only continue to grow as new models and versions of the existing models are released. ​ If you are not taking the time to experiment and learn from these models you are missing out. ​ My advice is to spend more time learning what AI is capable of and how it can help with your work. ​

​

Below is a list of AI LLM models. ​ Do not feel like you need to learn all of the different models. ​ Open AI is a great place to start, and use it to help with summarizing data, writing an Excel formula, or picking a graph to use in a presentation. ​

Ron's Recommendations

​

​

The Coaching Habit, Michael Bungay Stanier

​

When I was curious about coaching, I asked one of the best coaches I know (Nick Evans) for a book recommendation. Without missing a beat, he recommended this fantastic (and short) book.

​

The inside cover summarizes the book quite well. “This book is not about turning you into a coach. It’s about making you a leader, a manager, a human being who is more coach-like. Which means building the simple yet difficult habit.

​

  • Stay CURIOUS a little LONGER.
  • RUSH TO ACTION and advice giving MORE SLOWLY.”

​

It is about helping others find themselves and the best course of action (rather than give advice).

​

It provides 7 great coaching questions that help you truly take the time to be curious and help others find their own unique path. It reinforces how asking questions and listening is what coaching is all about:

​

  1. The kickstart question – What’s on your mind?
  2. The AWE question – And what else?
  3. The focus question – What’s the real challenge here for you?
  4. The foundation question – What do you want?
  5. The lazy question – How can I help?
  6. The strategic question – If you’re saying Yes to this, what are you saying No to?
  7. The learning question – what was most useful for you?

​

When I initially read some of these questions, I thought it was extremely simplistic. I decided to give it a test run and got marvelous results.

​

I would ask these questions and just listen and be patient.

​

The AWE question and the LAZY question are my favourites.

​

Asking the AWE question (‘and what else’) is a marvelous way to get deeper. Often times, the first answer to a question is a very surface level answer. If you ask this question the person you are coaching will then take the time to think and go deeper. If you give them space, it will be magic!

​

The LAZY question or (How can I help?) is also a fantastic open-ended question to help get deeper.

​

In our world where very few people truly listen, coaching using these simple questions and then listening (without rushing to advice giving) is truly a SUPERPOWER.
